lessons.title: Understand Statistical Questions
lessons.objective: I can tell the difference between a statistical question and a non-statistical question.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my reasoning using the words statistical question, data, variability, and survey.

concept.heading: What makes a question a statistical question?
concept.intro: A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data, and the answers are different for different people or cases. A non-statistical question has just one fixed answer.
concept.keyIdea: Statistical Questions & Variability. 1. Statistical Question: Expects answers that vary across people, trials, or items. 2. Non-Statistical Question: Has one single fixed answer. 3. Data Collection: Gather varied data points to create a distribution

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Question 1: "How many points did our top player score last night?" There is one player and one game, so there is one fixed answer, like 18 points.
One answer, no variety, so this is NOT a statistical question.
Question 2: "How many points does each player score per game?" The answers vary: 8, 12, 12, 15, 18, 20, 22.
Because the answers are different for different players, I must collect data. This IS a statistical question.
linesEs: Pregunta 1: «¿Cuántos puntos anotó anoche nuestro mejor jugador?» Hay un jugador y un partido, así que hay una sola respuesta fija, como 18 puntos.
Una sola respuesta, sin variación, así que esta no es una pregunta estadística.
Pregunta 2: «¿Cuántos puntos anota cada jugador por partido?» Las respuestas varían: 8, 12, 12, 15, 18, 20, 22.
Como las respuestas son distintas para distintos jugadores, tengo que reunir datos. Esta sí es una pregunta estadística.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: New question: "How many pets does each student in our class have?" Will every student give the same answer, or different answers?
Some students have 0 pets and others have 2 or 3, so the answers vary. Is this statistical or not statistical?
Now a different question: "How many days are in one week?" Does this have one fixed answer or many?
linesEs: Nueva pregunta: «¿Cuántas mascotas tiene cada estudiante de nuestra clase?» ¿Dará cada estudiante la misma respuesta o respuestas distintas?
Algunos estudiantes tienen 0 mascotas y otros tienen 2 o 3, así que las respuestas varían. ¿Es estadística o no estadística?
Ahora una pregunta diferente: «¿Cuántos días tiene una semana?» ¿Tiene una sola respuesta fija o muchas?

vocabulary.definition: A statistical question expects varied answers that can be collected as data.
vocabulary.example: How many minutes do students in our class read each night?

vocabulary.definition: A question answered with data that are expected to vary.
vocabulary.example: “How tall are the players on the team?” → answers vary: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in

vocabulary.definition: A question that has just one fixed answer that is the same no matter who you ask, so there is no data to collect.
vocabulary.example: “How tall am I?” → one answer: 60 in. Everyone who measures gets the same number.

vocabulary.definition: Facts and numbers you collect, like answers to a survey.
vocabulary.example: Player heights: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in — four different measurements

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.example: Scores 10, 12, 11 are close together (low variability); scores 2, 15, 30 are far apart (high variability)

vocabulary.definition: Collecting facts by asking people questions.
vocabulary.example: Asking 50 students 'What is your favorite sport?' and recording the answers

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.example: If most scores cluster in the middle with fewer at the edges, the distribution is symmetric

vocabulary.definition: A number line with one dot for each data value.
vocabulary.example: One dot for each answer, stacked above its value on the line.

lessons.title: Represent and Describe Data in a Histogram
lessons.objective: I can make and read a histogram to display data in intervals.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my histogram using the words histogram, frequency, interval, and distribution.

concept.heading: What is a histogram?
concept.intro: A histogram is a bar graph that groups numbers into equal ranges called intervals. The height of each bar is the frequency: how many values fall in that interval. The bars touch because the intervals are continuous.
concept.keyIdea: Histograms & Frequency Distributions. 1. Set equal intervals along the horizontal axis with no gaps. 2. Count the frequency (how many data values fall into each interval). 3. Draw adjacent bars with heights equal to frequency

worked.title: Watch me
lines: My data: 3, 7, 12, 15, 18, 24. I will use intervals of 10: 0–9, 10–19, 20–29.
Interval 0–9: the values 3 and 7 fit, so the frequency is 2.
Interval 10–19: the values 12, 15, and 18 fit, so the frequency is 3.
Interval 20–29: only the value 24 fits, so the frequency is 1.
Now I draw three bars with heights 2, 3, and 1, touching each other. The tallest bar (10–19) is where most values are.
linesEs: Mis datos: 3, 7, 12, 15, 18, 24. Voy a usar intervalos de 10: 0–9, 10–19, 20–29.
Intervalo 0–9: caben los valores 3 y 7, así que la frecuencia es 2.
Intervalo 10–19: caben los valores 12, 15 y 18, así que la frecuencia es 3.
Intervalo 20–29: solo cabe el valor 24, así que la frecuencia es 1.
Ahora dibujo tres barras con alturas 2, 3 y 1, tocándose entre sí. La barra más alta (10–19) es donde está la mayoría de los valores.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: New data: 2, 4, 8, 11, 13, 16, 21. We will use intervals of 10 again: 0–9, 10–19, 20–29.
How many values fall in 0–9? Count them. How many fall in 10–19?
How many fall in 20–29? Which interval would have the tallest bar?
linesEs: Datos nuevos: 2, 4, 8, 11, 13, 16, 21. Usaremos otra vez intervalos de 10: 0–9, 10–19, 20–29.
¿Cuántos valores caen en 0–9? Cuéntalos. ¿Cuántos caen en 10–19?
¿Cuántos caen en 20–29? ¿Cuál intervalo tendría la barra más alta?

vocabulary.definition: Group numerical data into intervals and show each interval's frequency with a bar.
vocabulary.example: Each touching bar shows how many values fall in one interval.

vocabulary.definition: A bar graph that groups data into equal ranges. The bars touch.
vocabulary.example: Bars side by side: 0-9 pts (3 players), 10-19 pts (8 players), 20-29 pts (4 players)

vocabulary.definition: How many times a value shows up.
vocabulary.example: If 5 players scored 10-19 points, the frequency for that interval is 5

vocabulary.definition: A range of numbers used to group data.
vocabulary.example: 0-9, 10-19, 20-29 are intervals of width 10 — each covers 10 values

vocabulary.definition: How the data is spread out.
vocabulary.example: Most data in the middle with fewer at the ends = bell-shaped; most on one side with a tail = skewed

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.example: Data in just 2 intervals = low variability. Data across 6 intervals = high variability

vocabulary.definition: A table that lists each interval and how many values fall in it.
vocabulary.example: 10–19 . . . 3 means three values are between 10 and 19.

vocabulary.definition: The pattern the bars or dots make across the intervals.
vocabulary.example: Tall in the middle and short on both sides is one shape.

vocabulary.definition: The tallest bar or stack in a data display.
vocabulary.example: The tallest bar of the histogram is the peak.

title: The Data Newsroom
mission: Investigate a question whose answers vary. Turn the data into an honest histogram and choose a headline the evidence supports.
investigate: Group the data into intervals of width 5. Count every value exactly once.
Move a value across an interval boundary. Which bars change?
Write a statistical question that could produce these data. Name the group and the measurement.
create: Write a newsroom report with a statistical question, a labeled histogram, and a headline. Explain one claim your graph cannot support.

support.prompt: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
support.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
feedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.

support.prompt: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How many innings are in a baseball game?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
support.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
feedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.

support.prompt: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because it asks about sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
support.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.
feedback: Sleep is a topic, not why it's statistical—which choice describes variability?
Hours are numbers, but are they used only in statistical questions?
If everyone slept 8 hours, would this be a statistical question?
hints: The question asks WHY it's statistical — focus on what happens when many students answer, not on the topic of sleep.
Think: if you asked every student how long they slept, would you get one number or many different numbers? That idea is called variability.
Picture asking 5 classmates their sleep hours and listing the numbers. Notice whether the list is all the same or varied — that's the key idea.

steps: Question: How tall is each player on the basketball team?
Student decision: This is NOT a statistical question.
Student reason: Height is just one number, so every answer will be the same.
support.explanation: The reason is wrong. The question asks about EACH player, and different players have different heights — for example 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, this IS a statistical question.
hints: The word "each" is a clue that you need data from many players.
Ask yourself: will every player give the same height, or different heights?

support.prompt: A histogram shows these frequencies: 0–4: 3 players, 5–9: 8 players, 10–14: 12 players, 15–19: 5 players. How many players are represented in total?
feedback: Add all frequencies: 3+8+12+5.
Did you count frequencies or find the highest value?
That total leaves out part of the data. Every bar contributes, so add all four frequencies together — including the shortest bar.
hints: The question asks for the TOTAL across all four intervals — not the tallest bar and not the biggest interval.
Each frequency counts the players in one interval, and no player is counted twice — so combine all four frequencies into one total.
Set up the addition: 3 + 8 + 12 + 5. The sum of all the bar heights is the total number of players.

support.prompt: In a histogram, what does the height of each bar represent?
choices: The frequency (count) of data in that interval
The average of the data in that interval
The range of the interval
The median of the data
support.explanation: Each bar's height shows the frequency — how many data values fall within that interval.
feedback: A bar height is not something you calculate from the values — it is something you tally. Think about what you would count to make the bar taller.
Height shows how many—does it show the typical value?
Range is the interval spread, not the height.
hints: Think about what you'd count to draw one bar: you'd tally how many data values land inside that interval.
Height is a COUNT, not a calculation — no averaging, no middle values. Ask which choice simply says 'how many.'
First step: imagine the interval 10–14 holding the values 11, 12, 12, 14. Its bar would rise to 4 — because 4 values fall inside.

support.prompt: How is a histogram different from a regular bar graph?
choices: Histogram bars touch (no gaps) because the intervals are continuous ranges
There is no difference
Histograms use colors and bar graphs don't
Bar graphs show numbers and histograms show words
support.explanation: In a histogram, bars touch because each interval connects to the next (0–9, 10–19, etc.) — the data is continuous.
feedback: There is a real structural difference between the two graphs. Look at the spacing between the bars and at what the horizontal axis is measuring.
Histograms always show intervals—this is the key difference.
Colors don't define a histogram—structure does.
hints: Picture both graphs side by side: one has spaces between its bars, one doesn't. Ask why that would be.
Think about the x-axis: categories like 'red, blue, green' can be separated, but number intervals like 0–9 and 10–19 connect end to end.
First step: write two neighboring intervals, 0–9 and 10–19. Notice that 10 starts right where 9 ends — that's why the bars behave differently.

support.prompt: A histogram has intervals: 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19. What is the width of each interval?
support.explanation: Each interval covers 5 values (0,1,2,3,4 then 5,6,7,8,9 etc.), so the width is 5.
feedback: The width is the span of each interval: 4−0=4 or 5−0=5.
That span covers two intervals joined together. Count the values inside a single interval, from its first number through its last.
Start is 0, end is 4—that's width 4, not 10.
hints: Width means how many whole-number values fit inside one interval — count them, don't just subtract the endpoints.
List the values in the first interval, 0–4: count every whole number from 0 up to and including 4.
Count aloud: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — how many numbers did you say? Check that the interval 5–9 holds the same amount.

steps: Data (points per game): 3, 7, 11, 13, 16, 22
Conclusion: So the histogram bars have heights 2, 2, and 1.
support.explanation: The student missed a value in the 10–19 interval. The values 11, 13, AND 16 all fall in 10–19, so its frequency is 3, not 2. The correct frequency counts are 0–9: 2 (the 3 and 7), 10–19: 3 (the 11, 13, and 16), and 20–29: 1 (the 22), which totals 6 — the same as the 6 data values.
hints: Count the data values first: 3, 7, 11, 13, 16, 22 is 6 values, but the frequencies add to only 5. A value was missed.
Check the 10–19 interval carefully — list every value from 10 to 19 in the data set.

support.prompt: Predict the range for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: Mean 9.25 · Median 8.5 · Range 11. Q1 6, Q3 13, IQR 7, MAD 3.3125. Quartiles use the median of each half.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: Data: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12. In a histogram with intervals 0–4, 5–9, and 10–14, what is the frequency in 5–9?
support.explanation: The values 5, 7, and 9 belong in 5–9. The 10 starts the next interval.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: Data: 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 8. How many observations are in the data set, including repeats?
support.explanation: Every measurement counts once. There are six observations, even though only three different values appear.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: A coach asks: "How many hours does each athlete on the track team sleep the night before a meet?" Why is this a statistical question?
choices: Because it is about sports
Because it has a numerical answer
Because the answers will vary from athlete to athlete
Because the coach asked it
core.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes sleep different amounts, so the data collected will vary.
feedback: Sports is a topic—what specific part makes this statistical?
Numbers can appear in fixed-answer questions too—why is this different?
Who asks the question doesn't determine if it's statistical—look deeper.
hints: Notice the words 'each athlete' — the coach plans to collect one number from every runner on the team.
Ask: will all athletes report the same hours of sleep? What we call it when collected answers differ is the key to this question.
Imagine the coach's list: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 hours from different athletes. The first step is naming what a changing list like that shows.

core.prompt: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: What time is it right now?
What is my shoe size?
What is 7 × 8?
How tall are the students in my class?
core.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — students' heights differ, so the data will vary.
feedback: What time it is right now doesn't vary—would collecting data help here?
Your shoe size is one fixed measurement—does it vary for different people?
Multiplication has one answer—would this question ever need data?
hints: Three of these have exactly one answer you could look up or compute. Find the one where collecting data from many people makes sense.
For each choice ask: 'If I surveyed my whole class, would I get a list of different numbers?' A statistical question needs that variety.
Test 'What is 7 × 8?' first — it has one answer no matter who you ask, so it can't be statistical. Apply the same test to the rest.

core.prompt: Which of these would collect data that VARIES (making it a statistical question)?
choices: How many siblings does each student in the class have?
How many days are in one week?
How many minutes are in one hour?
What is 12 + 12?
core.explanation: Number of siblings varies from student to student, so the collected data will vary — that makes it statistical. The others each have one fixed answer.
feedback: Days in a week is constant—does it vary?
Minutes in an hour don't change—does it vary?
12+12 always equals 24—would data vary?
hints: The capital word VARIES is the clue — you need the question whose answers change from student to student.
Check each choice: is it a fact of the calendar, clock, or math (never changes), or a survey where classmates would answer differently?
Start with 'How many days are in one week?' — that never changes, so its data can't vary. Keep testing each choice the same way.

steps: Question: How many points does the team need to win a game?
Student decision: This IS a statistical question.
Student reason: It is about basketball and the answer is a number, so it must be statistical.
core.explanation: The reason is wrong. Being about basketball or having a number does not make a question statistical. "How many points does the team need to win a game?" has one fixed answer — you only need to score more than the other team — so the answers do not vary. This is NOT a statistical question.
hints: Numbers and a sports topic do not automatically make a question statistical.
Ask whether the answers would VARY. If there is one fixed answer, it is not statistical.

core.prompt: A histogram of test scores shows: 50–59: 2, 60–69: 5, 70–79: 10, 80–89: 8, 90–99: 3. Which interval has the most students?
choices: 60–69 with 5 students
70–79 with 10 students
80–89 with 8 students
90–99 with 3 students
core.explanation: The 70–79 interval has the highest frequency of 10 students.
feedback: Compare: 2, 5, 10, 8, 3—the largest is 10.
5 is less than 10—which bar is tallest?
That interval holds the highest scores, but the question asks where the most students are. Compare the frequencies, not the score ranges.
hints: 'Most students' means the highest frequency — compare the counts 2, 5, 10, 8, 3, not the score ranges themselves.
Careful: the highest scores (90–99) don't mean the most students. Find the largest of the five frequencies first, then read off its interval.
First step: circle the largest number among 2, 5, 10, 8, 3. Then match that count back to its interval — and check the choice pairs both parts.

core.prompt: A histogram of goals-per-game shows: 0–1: 9 players, 2–3: 6, 4–5: 3, 6–7: 1. What shape is this distribution?
choices: Perfectly symmetric
Skewed right (most players low, tail toward high values)
Flat / uniform (all bars equal)
Skewed left (most players high, tail toward low values)
core.explanation: The tallest bars are at the low end (0–1) and the bars shrink as goals increase — the tail points right, so it is skewed right.
feedback: A symmetric shape would have the bars mirroring each other around the center. Compare the 9 at the low end with the 1 at the high end.
Are the bars roughly equal height? This isn't symmetric.
Most are low (left), tail goes high (right)—that's right skew.
hints: Sketch the bars: heights 9, 6, 3, 1 from left to right. Notice which side is tall and which way the heights trail off.
Skew is named for the TAIL — the long, low side — not for the peak. Find the direction the bars shrink toward, then name that direction.
First step: the tallest bar (9 players) is at 0–1 goals on the left, and heights fall to 1 by 6–7. Trace the tail with your finger, then name it.

steps: Data (assists per game): 1, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18
Intervals the student chose: 0–5, 6–10, 12–18
Frequency count: 0–5: 2, 6–10: 2, 12–18: 3
Conclusion: The student drew three bars and said the histogram was complete.
core.explanation: The intervals are not equal in width and they leave a gap. 0–5 and 6–10 each cover 6 values, but 12–18 covers 7 values and the value 11 has no bin at all. Histogram intervals must be equal-width and cover every value with no gaps. Using equal intervals of 5 (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19) gives frequencies 0–4: 2 (the 1 and 4), 5–9: 2 (the 6 and 9), 10–14: 1 (the 12), and 15–19: 2 (the 15 and 18), totaling 7.
hints: Check the width of each interval the student used. Are 0–5, 6–10, and 12–18 all the same size?
Where would a value of 11 go? Every value needs exactly one equal-width bin — there can be no gaps.

core.prompt: Predict the range for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: Mean 9.375 · Median 8.5 · Range 10. Q1 6, Q3 13, IQR 7, MAD 3.2188. Quartiles use the median of each half.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: Data: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12. In a histogram with intervals 0–4, 5–9, and 10–14, what is the frequency in 5–9?
core.explanation: The values 5, 7, and 9 belong in 5–9. The 10 starts the next interval.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: Data: 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 8. How many observations are in the data set, including repeats?
core.explanation: Every measurement counts once. There are six observations, even though only three different values appear.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.prompt: A survey asks 30 students how many books they read last month, collecting 30 answers. What makes this a statistical question?
choices: It is about books
Everyone reads the same number
The answers vary from student to student
It has exactly one correct answer
stretch.explanation: Statistical questions anticipate variability in the data collected across many people.
feedback: A topic doesn't determine if a question is statistical—what else matters?
If everyone read the same number, would this be statistical?
One answer means fixed, not statistical—but do the answers vary here?
hints: Re-read the setup: 30 students each report how many books they read — that's 30 separate answers collected.
Ask what those 30 answers probably look like: all identical, or a mix like 2, 5, 0, 7...? That property is what makes a question statistical.
First step: picture the list of 30 numbers. Decide whether the list is fixed or full of different values, then match that idea to a choice.

stretch.prompt: Which rewrite turns 'What is my resting heart rate?' into a statistical question?
choices: Is my heart rate high?
What is a heart rate?
What are the resting heart rates of students in my class?
What is the teacher's heart rate?
stretch.explanation: Asking across many people, whose rates vary, makes the question statistical.
feedback: This still asks about one person—does one person's answer vary?
This still asks about one person—will the answer vary?
One person's rate doesn't vary—will you get different answers?
hints: The original question asks about ONE person's resting heart rate — one measurement, so no variability.
A statistical rewrite must gather data from many people whose numbers differ. Check each choice: how many people does it measure?
Test the first rewrite, 'Is my heart rate high?' — still one person, still one answer. Keep checking until a choice surveys a whole group.

steps: Question: How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?
Student says: This is NOT a statistical question.
Reason: It only asks about one player, so there is no variability.
stretch.explanation: Even though it asks about one player, "this season" means multiple games. The number of touchdowns per game varies, so there IS variability in the data. This IS a statistical question.
hints: Think about whether the data collected would have different values across games.
The question asks about performance over a whole season — each game can have a different result.

stretch.prompt: Write one statistical question and one non-statistical question about your school's cafeteria. Explain why each question is or is not statistical, and describe what the data would look like for the statistical question.
stretch.frame: Statistical question: ___. This is statistical because ___. The data might look like: ___. Non-statistical question: ___. This is not statistical because ___.
stretch.explanation: A strong statistical cafeteria question asks about each person, such as 'How many minutes does each student wait in the lunch line?' — the data would be a spread of values like 2, 5, 7, and 11 minutes. A non-statistical one, such as 'How many tables are in the cafeteria?', has a single fixed answer, so there is nothing to collect or compare.
hints: You need TWO questions about the cafeteria: one where classmates would answer differently, and one with a single fixed answer.
Brainstorm cafeteria data: minutes in line, lunches bought per week. For the non-statistical one, use a fixed fact like the number of tables.
Start your first sentence: 'How many ___ does each student ___?' Using 'each student' builds in variability — then describe the different answers.

stretch.prompt: A histogram of points-per-game has its tallest bars on the LEFT (low scores) and a long tail stretching RIGHT toward a few high scorers. How is this distribution described?
choices: Skewed left
Symmetric
Bimodal (two equal peaks)
Skewed right
stretch.explanation: The tail points right (toward the high values), so it is skewed right — most players are clustered at the low end.
feedback: It is tempting to name a skew after where the tall bars sit. A skew is named for the direction the long tail stretches instead.
Left skew has the tail on the left, not right.
Symmetric means roughly equal—this has a clear tail.
hints: Underline the two location words in the stem: tallest bars on the LEFT, long tail stretching RIGHT. Skew is named after one of those.
Rule: a distribution is skewed in the direction its TAIL stretches, not where its peak sits. Decide which way the tail points here.
First step: the stem says the tail stretches toward the few high scorers. Apply the tail rule to name the skew — don't follow the peak.

stretch.prompt: Two histograms show the SAME 40 test scores — one uses intervals of 5, the other intervals of 20. Which statement is true?
choices: The interval-of-5 histogram has more bars and shows more detail about the shape
The interval-of-5 histogram leaves some scores out
The interval-of-20 histogram has more bars
Both histograms must look exactly the same
stretch.explanation: Smaller intervals create more bars and reveal finer detail; larger intervals smooth the shape into fewer bars. Both still include all 40 scores.
feedback: Changing the interval width regroups the data but never throws any of it away — all 40 scores still land in some bar.
Wider intervals gather more values into each bar, so they produce fewer bars. Think about how many 20-wide bins it takes to cover the same range.
Smaller intervals show more detail—more bars, finer shape.
hints: Both histograms use all 40 scores — the only difference is bucket width: 5 points vs 20 points per interval.
Reason it out: covering the same score range with narrower buckets requires MORE buckets. Then ask what having more bars does for detail.
First step: take the range 60–79. With width 20 it's ONE bar; with width 5 it becomes four bars (60–64, 65–69, 70–74, 75–79). Compare the detail.

steps: Conclusion: The histogram is symmetric because the bars go 1, 2, 3, 4, 2.
stretch.explanation: The frequencies are correct (1, 2, 3, 4, 2), but this is NOT symmetric. In a symmetric histogram, the bars rise and fall evenly from the center. Here the bars increase from left to right and only drop at the end — the data is skewed LEFT (most scores are on the higher end).
hints: Symmetric means the left side mirrors the right side. Does 1, 2, 3, 4, 2 mirror evenly?
The peak (4) is in the 80–89 range, which is toward the right. That means most data is on the high end.

stretch.prompt: A teacher collected test scores and made two different histograms — one with intervals of 5 (50–54, 55–59, etc.) and one with intervals of 20 (50–69, 70–89, 90–109). Both use the same data. How might the two histograms look different? Which interval size gives you more detail about the distribution? When might the larger interval be better?
stretch.frame: The histogram with intervals of 5 would have ___ bars and show ___. The histogram with intervals of 20 would have ___ bars and show ___. Smaller intervals are better when ___, and larger intervals are better when ___.
stretch.explanation: Intervals of 5 across 50–109 make 12 narrow bars with small frequencies, so peaks, gaps, and the exact shape show up clearly. Intervals of 20 make only 3 tall bars that smooth those details away, which is useful when the data set is large or you only want the big-picture comparison of low, middle, and high scores.
hints: Same data, two bucket sizes. Think: chopping scores into many small buckets vs a few big buckets — what changes about the picture?
Compare three things: how many bars each histogram has, how tall its bars get, and how clearly you can see the shape, peaks, or gaps.
Start with a count: intervals of 5 covering 50–109 make 12 bars; intervals of 20 make just 3. Write what 12 skinny bars reveal that 3 wide ones hide.
